claims: Americans can acquire Canadian citizenship primarily through descent or naturalization.
Bill C-3 expands eligibility beyond the previous first-generation limit for citizenship by descent.
Bill C-3 allows those with a Canadian parent or grandparent to prove an unbroken line of citizenship.
Many Americans with a Canadian ancestor (parent or grandparent) can claim citizenship following Bill C-3.
Applicants must apply for a Citizenship Certificate from Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) to obtain proof of citizenship.
Permanent residence can be obtained through work, family sponsorship, or economic immigration (e.g., Express Entry).
Permanent residents must be physically present in Canada for at least 1,095 days (3 years) out of the five years preceding the citizenship application.
Naturalization applicants must file personal income tax for at least three years within the five-year period.
Naturalization requires demonstrating proficiency in English or French.
Naturalization requires passing a test regarding Canadian history, geography, government, and rights.
The language and knowledge tests for naturalization apply to applicants aged 18–54.
Americans can hold both U.S. and Canadian citizenship.
Proving citizenship by descent requires official, unbroken documentation, such as birth, marriage, or adoption certificates.
A criminal record (including some misdemeanors like DUI) can make an American inadmissible to Canada.
